title: The Compass: Finding Tomorrow in the Minds of Yesterday
gist: A promotional review of Sunil Mehta's young-adult novel The Compass, in which four students time-travel into the minds of Einstein, Robert Noyce and Steve Jobs; it argues the book makes innovation feel human and accessible. No market-relevant data beyond the Kindle edition being a category bestseller.

insights.claim: Sunil Mehta's novel The Compass follows four students who use a compass to enter the minds of Albert Einstein, Robert Noyce and Steve Jobs, representing science, computing technology and product design.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.quote: Their encounters with Albert Einstein, Robert Noyce and Steve Jobs offer an imaginative route into the human experiences behind scientific and technological change.

insights.claim: The reviewer argues that seeing innovation from inside the inventor's doubts, rather than as inevitable outcomes, makes breakthroughs feel accessible to young readers and frames technology as the result of human choices.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Soft argument for STEM-education narratives; no market signal.
insights.quote: It encourages readers to see technology as the outcome of human choices.
